title: Mindful life: Don’t forget to invite your mates to your cosy night in
gist: Personal essay arguing that social connection is the most neglected health metric: influencer-driven 'cosy night in' self-care consumerism promotes isolation, whereas genuine hygge centres on hosting others. Cites declining in-person socialising in OECD countries and a 70% fall in regular hosting in the US over 50 years.

themes.theme: Social connection as an ignored health metric

insights.claim: Studies suggest a lack of social connection poses a health risk comparable to obesity, smoking and high blood pressure.
insights.speaker: Sarah Collins
insights.so_what: Loneliness framed as a public-health risk factor on par with major chronic-disease drivers; relevant to health-tech and wellbeing spending.

insights.claim: Consumers spend heavily tracking body metrics such as blood sugar, heart rate and sleep quality, yet social connection is the one health indicator people largely ignore.
insights.speaker: Sarah Collins
insights.so_what: Gap in the wellness-tracking market: connection is unmeasured while biometric tracking is monetised.
insights.quote: social connection is the one indicator of health that we rather curiously ignore

insights.claim: Social media influencers push lonely people to buy products such as scented candles and soft blankets to create cosy vibes, which the author found deepened rather than relieved isolation and rumination.

insights.claim: The Danish practice of hygge fundamentally involves hosting friends and family, but has been co-opted and corrupted by influencers into a solitary cosy-night-in aesthetic.
insights.speaker: Sarah Collins
insights.so_what: Cultural trends repackaged as solo consumption miss the social core; watch for 'social' rebranding of wellness.
